description:
Solo team from Sapporo, Japan. I'm a software developer who likes building tools on top of real data.

I'm working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: a web app that shows which landing sites still have sunlight and a direct link to Earth when the landing date slips, using JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA terrain.

Not looking for members this time.
summary:
Lunar missions rarely land on the date they first planned. When the date or the site moves, planners have to ask again whether the lander will have sunlight for power and the Earth in view for a direct link, and today that means going back and forth between several expert tools.

Skimline answers that question on one screen. Its slip chart puts sites down the side and landing dates across, and colors every landing time by whether the mission requirements still hold. Clicking a cell shows the sky from that site: the terrain skyline from LRO LOLA data, the paths of the Sun and Earth, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset.

It runs in a browser with no server, and its numbers are checked against JPL Horizons and against missions that already flew.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

- Slip chart. Rows are landing sites, columns are landing dates. Each cell is one landing time, colored by go / no-go, hours of power after landing, share of the mission with power or an Earth link, or the longest darkness. This is the view for "the launch moved by two weeks, which sites still work?"

- Sky panorama. The 360-degree skyline seen from the site, with the paths of the Sun and Earth over the mission and their current positions. Cards show "Sunset in 3 d 4 h" and "Earthset in 11 h". Two sites can be stacked for the same moment.

- Mission timeline. Power and Earth visibility as bars, one row per site, with a scrubber and playback.

- Requirements. Mission length, height of the array and antenna, array type and pointing, how long the battery can bridge darkness, how much link time is needed. The verdict follows from these, together with the battery capacity needed for the longest dark gap.

- Site list and map. Past landings and south pole candidates with the source of every coordinate, custom coordinates, and a shaded-relief map of the south pole where a click adds a site.

- Examples. South pole candidates, SLIM (January 2024), Blue Ghost Mission 1 (March 2025), Chang'e 4 on the far side.

HOW IT WORKS

- Sun and Earth. Hourly positions in the Moon-fixed frame for 2023 to 2035 are taken from JPL Horizons ahead of time and shipped with the app. Azimuth and elevation at any site are computed from those vectors in the browser, including the parallax of the Earth and its libration.

- Skyline. South of 82 S the skyline comes from LRO LOLA elevation models. From the site, rays march outward along great circles for 300 km and keep the highest elevation angle for every 0.25 degrees of azimuth. Positions are handled in 3D, so the curvature of the Moon is included, and there is no refraction to correct for. The listed polar sites use the 5 m model. Any other point, such as one picked on the map, is computed in about a second in a Web Worker from 40 m, 80 m and 320 m tiles.

- Power. The share of the Sun's disk above the skyline times the cosine of the angle on the array. The array can track the Sun, lie flat, or be fixed at a given azimuth and tilt.

- Earth link. The Earth's center has to clear the skyline by a chosen margin.

HOW I CHECKED IT

The app has a Validation tab that shows these with their sources, and one command rebuilds every number.

- Against JPL Horizons: 264 samples at 12 sites from the equator to within 0.1 degrees of the pole. The largest error is 0.006 degrees in both azimuth and elevation. The Sun is 0.53 degrees across.

- Blue Ghost Mission 1: the tool gives 348 hours from landing to sunset. Firefly reports 346 hours of daylight operations.

- SLIM: JAXA reported that the solar cells faced west while the Sun was in the east, and that operations resumed on January 28, 2024 after the Sun moved west. With a fixed west-facing array the tool shows no power at landing, light returning on January 23 and half output on January 26. The real attitude was more complex than a vertical plate, so this checks the geometry, not the exact date.

- Chang'e 4: the Earth never rises above -37 degrees, so no direct link at any date.

- Terrain resolution: the 40 m tiles differ from the 5 m model by 0.07 to 0.16 degrees on average and overstate yearly sunlight by 0.2 to 2.9 points at the three polar sites. That is why the listed sites use the 5 m model, and the page says which model each skyline came from.

- Illumination level: the connecting ridge near Shackleton gets 85% mean sunlight in 2027. Noda et al. (2008) report 86% for the best-lit surface at the south pole from the KAGUYA (SELENE) laser altimeter.

WHAT IT DOES NOT MODEL

Terrain north of 82 S (smooth sphere there), ground station visibility on Earth, temperature, dust, and shadows cast by the lander itself. The 5 m LOLA model is mostly interpolated between laser tracks, so features smaller than a few tens of meters are not resolved.

WHO IT IS FOR

Mission planners who need a first answer in minutes when a date or a site moves, and students or the public who want to see why the lunar south pole is hard: the Sun and the Earth both skim the skyline, and a few days or a few kilometers decide the outcome.

BENEFITS

- Many sites and landing dates on one chart, so the cost of a slip is visible at a glance.

- Every verdict comes with its reason: power or link, and the sky that explains it.

- The requirements are adjustable, so the same chart serves different landers.

- The numbers are checked against flown missions and can be rebuilt with one command.

- Nothing to install. It runs from a static page.

WHAT I HOPE TO ACHIEVE

Make the effect of a schedule slip visible early, so a team can rule sites in or out before spending time on detailed analysis. The next steps are ground station visibility, relay satellites, temperature, and the north pole.

BUILT WITH

TypeScript, React, Vite, Canvas 2D and Web Workers. Data preparation runs in Node.js with geotiff.js. Tests use Vitest. Hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages.

Code: https://github.com/Atamol/Skimline

AI tools were used for coding.
